classification.subject: Physics
classification.chapter: Chapter 8: Force and Laws of Motion

learning_objectives: State Newton's three laws of motion
Apply F=ma to solve simple numerical problems
prerequisites: Basic understanding of speed and velocity

concepts.name: Inertia
concepts.explanation: The tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion.

concepts.name: Force
concepts.explanation: A push or pull that can change an object's velocity.

concepts.name: Momentum
concepts.explanation: The product of an object's mass and velocity, p=mv.

definitions.name: Newton's First Law
definitions.explanation: An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force.

definitions.name: Newton's Second Law
definitions.explanation: The rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied force: F=ma.

examples: A ball rolling on a frictionless surface
A car accelerating when the engine applies force
applications: Seatbelts and inertia in vehicle safety
Rocket propulsion using Newton's third law

common_misconceptions.correction: In the absence of air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A moving object needs a continuous force to keep moving.
common_misconceptions.correction: An object in motion stays in motion unless acted upon by a net external force (Newton's First Law).

teaching_plan.rationale: Three 40-minute periods: one per law, given moderate concept density and a need for worked numerical practice.

periods.title: Newton's First Law & Inertia
periods.pacing_notes: Spend extra time on misconception that motion requires continuous force.

periods.title: Momentum & Newton's Third Law
objectives: Relate momentum to force and motion

period_content.entry_ticket: Why does a passenger lurch forward when a bus stops suddenly?
period_content.teacher_script: Begin by asking students to push a book across the desk and observe it slowing down...
period_content.blackboard_notes: Inertia = resistance to change in motion. Newton's 1st Law: no net force -> no change in velocity.
checkpoint_questions: Why does the coin drop into the glass when the card is flicked?
Give one everyday example of inertia.
period_content.exit_ticket: Explain in your own words why seatbelts are necessary.
period_content.homework: Find 3 examples of inertia at home and describe them.
period_content.mentor_moment: Astronauts experience near-zero friction in space, which is why Newton's first law feels almost visible there.

period_content.entry_ticket: If you push a shopping cart with double the force, what happens to its acceleration?
period_content.teacher_script: Introduce F=ma with a simple cart-and-weights demonstration...
period_content.blackboard_notes: F = m × a. Units: Force (N), mass (kg), acceleration (m/s^2).
period_content.classroom_activity_summary: Measure acceleration of a cart under different applied forces.
checkpoint_questions: A 2kg object accelerates at 3 m/s^2. Find the force.
What happens to acceleration if mass doubles and force stays constant?
period_content.homework: Complete 5 F=ma numerical problems from the textbook.
period_content.mentor_moment: Formula One engineers use F=ma every day to balance engine power against car mass.

period_content.entry_ticket: Why does a rocket move forward by pushing gas backward?
period_content.teacher_script: Connect momentum conservation to Newton's third law using a balloon-rocket demo...
period_content.blackboard_notes: p = m × v. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
period_content.classroom_activity_summary: Balloon rocket demonstration of action-reaction pairs.
checkpoint_questions: State Newton's third law in your own words.
Why does a gun recoil when fired?
period_content.exit_ticket: Give one example of momentum conservation.
period_content.homework: Write a short paragraph connecting all three laws using one real-world scenario.
period_content.mentor_moment: Rocket scientist tip: every space launch is a live demonstration of Newton's third law.

activities.title: Coin and Card Inertia Trick
instructions: Place the card on top of the glass.
Place the coin on the card.
Flick the card horizontally and observe the coin drop into the glass.
success_criteria: Student can explain why the coin doesn't move with the card.

activities.title: Cart Force Lab
instructions: Attach different weights to the cart.
Measure time to travel 1m and calculate acceleration.
success_criteria: Students correctly calculate acceleration from measured data.

activities.title: Balloon Rocket Race
instructions: Thread a straw onto a string across the room.
Tape an inflated balloon to the straw.
Release and observe the balloon's motion.
success_criteria: Students identify the action and reaction forces involved.

written_questions.question: Explain why a passenger tends to fall forward when a car suddenly brakes.
written_questions.answer_key: Due to inertia, the passenger's body continues moving forward even as the car stops.
written_questions.rubric: 1 pt for mentioning inertia, 1 pt for correct direction of motion.

mcqs.question: If force is doubled and mass stays constant, acceleration:
mcqs.explanation: F=ma means a is directly proportional to F.

written_questions.question: A 4kg object experiences a net force of 20N. Find its acceleration.
written_questions.rubric: 1 pt formula, 1 pt correct substitution, 1 pt correct answer with units.

mcqs.question: Newton's Third Law states that forces occur in:
mcqs.explanation: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction, forming a pair.

written_questions.question: Explain how a rocket accelerates in space where there is nothing to push against.
written_questions.answer_key: The rocket pushes exhaust gas backward, and by Newton's third law the gas pushes the rocket forward; no external medium is needed.
written_questions.rubric: 2 pts for correctly applying Newton's third law, 1 pt for clarity.

learning_gaps.misconception: A moving object needs a continuous force to keep moving.
learning_gaps.diagnostic_question: Ask: 'What happens to a hockey puck sliding on frictionless ice with no force applied?'
learning_gaps.remedial_action: Use frictionless-surface thought experiments and video simulations to isolate the role of friction.

learning_gaps.misconception: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones.
learning_gaps.diagnostic_question: Ask: 'Which falls faster: a hammer or a feather, on the Moon?'
learning_gaps.remedial_action: Show the Apollo 15 hammer-feather drop video and discuss the role of air resistance.
